catalog_quote: 0. Introduction. Of special interest in this Paya dialect of Kuna¹ is the stress sandhi. In routine speech, stress usually occurs on the penultimate syllable, but stress is changed to the last syllabe [sic] when the word is emphasized. Also, a noun will be stressed on the last syllable, if, when functioning as object, it provides new information ... the syllable with sentence stress has an extra-high pitch. ... 1.1. Stress in routine speech. In routine speech stress is, for the most part, predictable. In fact in 2. — 8. stress occurs on the penultimate syllable in all words. Therefore stress has been written only in 1. Disyllabic words are stressed on the first syllable, as in: mdéi ‘boy’, dme ‘woman’, dri ‘iguana’, déte ‘puppy’, tédo ‘to play’. In trisyllabic words, the stress usually occurs on the second syllable, as in: omégan ‘women’, maéimal ‘boys’, eétko ‘will untie’, balbirki ‘sloth’, nujdbak ‘with an egg’. Stress may occur on the first syllable of a three-syllable word, especially in words which, in their shortened forms, lose the last vowel, as in: ¢mala or imal ‘things’, dpéala or dpéal ...
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: In routine (non-emphatic) speech, word stress falls on the penultimate syllable: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable, trisyllables on the second; stress is predictable. Under emphasis, or when an object noun conveys new information, stress moves to the final syllable ('stress sandhi'); the syllable carrying sentence stress gets extra-high pitch. Corroborated second-hand for the Colombian (Caimán Nuevo) variety by Llerena 1986: 48 ('en la palabra aislada recae, con muy pocas excepciones, en la penúltima sílaba. Los sintagmas dañan esta tendencia').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the recovered snippets (for San Blas Kuna, Smith 2014: 49 reports secondary stress on the penult of words longer than four syllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the final syllable when a word is emphasized and on an object noun that provides new information; 'stress may occur on the first syllable of a three-syllable word, especially in words which, [..]' (condition cut off in the snippet); Llerena adds 'con muy pocas excepciones' and that phrases (sintagmas) disturb the penultimate tendency.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, 'routine speech' (citation/normal register); the article is centrally about stress sandhi at phrase/sentence level (emphatic and information-structure shifts, extra-high pitch on sentence stress). Paya dialect, Darién, Panama, 600-800 speakers per the article.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Paya dialect (villages of Paya and Púcuro, Darién, Panama; 600-800 speakers), which is the Panamanian side of Border Kuna [kvn] = bord1248. Llerena's corroborating statement is for the Kuna of Caimán Nuevo (Antioquia, Colombia), also kvn. Smith 2014 and Holmer 1947 (held by the project, also penultimate/weight-based) describe San Blas Kuna (sanb1242), not this language.

new_statements.quote: [fn. 1, p. 1] Stress or accent is not normally written in Kuna, but is marked here on some words to help the beginning student. [17.2.2.3, p. 229] Stress switch. An action may be dramatized and intensified by a change of stress. This intensification is achieved by changing a lenis consonant to fortis, and stressing the final syllable of the emphasized word. Examples 1. Purkwis. 'It died.' becomes Purkwís. 'It dropped dead.' 2. chibu 'white' becomes chipú 'snow-white' 3. Nade. 'He went.' becomes Naté. 'He took off/disappeared.' [18.4.5.2, p. 250] If the evaluatory adjective is descriptive, the short form is used, and the stress changes to the last syllable of the adjective. Derived adjectives do not change their stress.
new_statements.citation: Forster, D. Keith. 2011. Paya Kuna: An introductory grammar. SIL Language and Culture Documentation and Description 14. Dallas: SIL International. xi+320 pp.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted passages found verbatim in the text: fn. 1 'Stress or accent is not normally written in Kuna, but is marked here on some words to help the beginning student.' (the text layerprinted p. 1); 17.2.2.3 'Stress switch. An action may be dramatized and intensified by a change of stress. This intensification is achieved by changing a lenis consonant to fortis, and stressing the final syllable of the emphasized word.' with examples Purkwis->Purkwís, chibu->chipú, Nade->Naté (lines 11209-11216, page before running header '230 Telling Stories' = p. 229); 18.4.5.2 'If the evaluatory adjective is descriptive, the short form is used, and the stress changes to the last syllable of the adj…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate record (Pike, Forster & Forster 1986: penultimate in routine speech, shifted to the last syllable under emphasis): the same author here describes the same emphatic shift to the final syllable (17.2.2.3) and adds the post-predicate evaluatory-adjective shift and negative-suffix stress; it does not itself state the penultimate default, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the placement, only the sandhi/shift detail.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The pedagogical grammar never states where word stress falls by default. It treats stress as real but unwritten (accent marks added only on some words for learners), refers to 'the stressed syllable' when describing vowel length (1.2.3.3, 2.2.4), and describes stress SHIFT to the final syllable (with lenis->fortis) for dramatization/intensification (17.2.2.3) and for descriptive evaluatory adjectives in post-predicate position (totó, tatár; 18.4.5.2); negative suffix -juli/-chuli attracts stress to its first syllable (olobijúli) or to the preceding syllable in the idiomatic-antithesis use (ichéjuli) (9.4.2.2-3, p. 107); emphatic túmmad has 'heavy stress' (fn. 110). The accent marks the book does write fall overwhelmingly on word-final vowels (ajáj, anná, walpá/kakapá 'three/-teen', totó, yopí, purkwís, chipú, naté), i.e. the marked cases are final stress, consistent with an unmarked non-final (penultimate) default, but that default is my inference, not a statement in the text.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress under emphasis/dramatization (Purkwís, chipú, Naté); final stress on short-form descriptive evaluatory adjectives in post-predicate position (totó, tatár), derived adjectives keep their stress; stress on the negative suffix (olobijúli) or the syllable before it (ichéjuli); emphatic túmmad with heavy initial stress and lengthened mm; word-timing compresses long words (1.2.3.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Forster 2011 describes Paya Kuna as spoken in Paya, Pucuro and Capeti (Darien, Panama) and in Arquia and Kudi (Colombia) = Border Kuna bord1248; Forster 1977 fn. 1 identifies 'Border Cuna' as a dialect of Cuna also called Colombia Cuna, Darien Cuna, Long-haired Cuna or Paya Cuna (c. 800 speakers), data from Paya 1974. Both are the same variety as the catalog's Pike, Forster & Forster 1986 'Paya dialect of Kuna'.

sources.note: 'As a general rule, the penultimate syllable of a Kuna word is stressed (Smith 2014: 48-9). In stressed open syllables, vowels are automatically long (Llerena Villalobos 2000: 66; Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 62)'; 'There is neither tone nor distinctive vowel nasality in Kuna.' Secondary synthesis of Kuna in general.

sources.citation: Smith, Wikaliler Daniel. 2014. A grammar of Guna: a community-centered approach. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin. Sec. 2.5 Stress, pp. 48-49.
sources.note: San Blas/Gardi Guna (sanb1242), not Border Kuna: 'In roots, the stress always falls on the penultimate (second to last) syllable'; clitics do not affect main stress; secondary stress on the penult in words longer than four syllables. p. 25 notes Forster 1977 proposed 'Border Guna' as a separate language.

sources.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1947. Critical and comparative grammar of the Cuna language. Etnologiska Studier 14. Göteborg: Etnografiska Museet. Sec. 4 Syllabification and accent, pp. 19-24.
sources.note: San Blas Cuna (consultant Pérez Kantule): 'the Cuna stress system.. depends altogether on the nature of the syllables.. no free accentuation.. The accent thus bears evenly on all long vowels or short vowels followed by a double or geminated consonant.. final closed syllables are never marked with an accent' (p. 23). No Paya/Colombian data.
